Ultrasound of tubular structure with echogenic walls in dilated small bowel 👉🏼 ascariasis

1) the name of the worm is Ascaris lumbricoides
2) an estimated 1 billion people are infected, but it is more common in tropical and subtropical areas
3) clumps of worms in the bowel can lead to bowel obstruction (as in this case) or intussusception

0 - No GVHD rash
1 - Maculopapular rash &amp;lt;25% body surface area
2 - Maculopapular rash 25-50% ESA
3 - Maculopapular rash &amp;gt; 50% BSA
4 - Generalized erythroderma (&amp;gt;50% BSA) plus bullous formation or desquamation &amp;gt; 5% BSA

<a class="image-link image-link-6137 position-relative" data-bookmarked="false" data-bookmarks="0" data-caption="Guide to Interpretation of Positive Blood Cultures

I arrange the potential Gram stain results that one can be called w/ as follows: Gram(+) cocci, Gram(+) rods, Gram(–) rods, Gram(–) cocci, yeast. Gram(+) cocci are grouped by ‘morphology’ since the lab usually tells you this: clusters, pairs, chains, etc. Fill in with orgs.

The orgs are deliberately ordered this way: Gram(+) orgs are often [skin] contaminants, Gram(–) orgs &amp;amp; yeast are not. Remember that clinician adjudication is the ‘gold standard’ for deciding what is a contaminant!

Now, w/ the bugs organized, when you get that call from the micro lab, here are 3 questions to ask yourself/the lab:
1) Number of positive bottles/cultures and time to positivity?
2) ‘Shape’ of the bacteria?
3) Aerobic or anaerobic bottle?

Fewer positive cultures &amp;amp; longer time to positivity suggests a contaminant. Apply Q1) to Gram(+) orgs. Time to positivity tough to interpret unless extreme (ex. 8h v 48h). Can use Number of positive cx fact to your advantage – before abx, obtain more cx &amp;amp; increase the denominator!

Apply Q2) to Gram(+) rods since their shapes are so distinct. There are some uniquely shaped Gram(–) rods too, but rare (think Fusobacterium). Here’s a comparative chart of GPRs to illustrate. A great reason to go to micro lab and review the Gram stain!

Apply Q3) to Gram(+) rods &amp;amp; perhaps Gram(–) rods too. For GPRs, preferential growth in the aerobic v anaerobic bottle helps organize the ‘shape’ chart. Ex: while you await speciation for that aerobic box car shaped GPR, these clues suggest Bacillus, usually a contaminant!

For Gram(–) rods, the pearl is that Pseudomonas is a ‘strict’ aerobe and ought to grow preferentially in the aerobic bottle – thus, a GNR that grows in the anaerobic bottle first is less likely Pseudomonas. Of course, always exceptions to these pearls, so await speciation!

Dr. Varun Phadke @ &amp;lt;a href=&amp;#34;https://twitter.com/VarunPhadke2&amp;#34;&amp;gt;https://twitter.com/VarunPhadke2&amp;lt;/a&amp;gt;

<a class="image-link image-link-6136 position-relative" data-bookmarked="false" data-bookmarks="0" data-caption="Pudendal Neuralgia
• Pudendal nerve arises from S2-S4 roots and innervates perineal structures
• Nerve is prone to entrapment at 2 sites:
  1) Ischial spine by compression of sacrospinous &amp;amp; sacrotuberous ligaments (green arrow)
  2) Pudendal (Alcock) canal (yellow arrow)
• Pudendal neuralgia usually occurs in women w/ prior pelvic surgery but can occur in men &amp;amp; women cyclists
• CT-guidance is a terrific method to provide a nerve block
• A positive pudendal nerve block can help diagnose pudendal neuralgia &amp;amp; provide therapeutic benefit
• Important to diagnose correctly, as many patients see multiple providers before arriving at correct diagnosis

Dr. Mark Mamlouk @ &amp;lt;a href=&amp;#34;https://twitter.com/MarkMamloukMD&amp;#34;&amp;gt;https://twitter.com/MarkMamloukMD&amp;lt;/a&amp;gt;

<a class="image-link image-link-6135 position-relative" data-bookmarked="false" data-bookmarks="0" data-caption="Ipilimumab-Induced Hypophysitis. 
Pituitary gland enlargement occurs on therapy &amp;amp; resolves after therapy.
 - Ipilimumab is a monoclonal antibody that blocks cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen-4, and adverse events may occur due increased T-cell activation.
 - Clinically, patients can develop anterior hypopituitarism.
 - On imaging, pituitary enlargement is the main finding, while stalk thickening can also be seen.
 - Resolves after therapy.
 - History of drug therapy important to not mistake for a metastasis.

Dr. Mark Mamlouk @ &amp;lt;a href=&amp;#34;https://twitter.com/MarkMamloukMD&amp;#34;&amp;gt;https://twitter.com/MarkMamloukMD&amp;lt;/a&amp;gt;

<a class="image-link image-link-6134 position-relative" data-bookmarked="false" data-bookmarks="0" data-caption="Krabbe Disease 

Check out this interesting case of Krabbe disease, a rare genetic leukodystrophy. Diagnosis was made by radiology, which helped guide confirmatory lab testing and expedite treatment with clinical trials. 

• Autosomal recessive leukodystrophy w/ deficiency of galactocerebroside that leads to accumulation of psychosine, which is neurotoxic 
• Symptoms: dev delay, seizures, visual failure, cerebellar ataxia 
Imaging shows 
• Symmetric abnormal WM, cerebellar nuclei, &amp;amp; PLICs 
• Mineralization of thalami 
• Enlarged optic nerves (from globoid cell deposition) 
• Dec NAA, inc Cho 
Tx: Stem cell transplant, clinical trials 

Dr. Mark Mamlouk @ &amp;lt;a href=&amp;#34;https://twitter.com/MarkMamloukMD&amp;#34;&amp;gt;https://twitter.com/MarkMamloukMD&amp;lt;/a&amp;gt;

<a class="image-link image-link-6132 position-relative" data-bookmarked="false" data-bookmarks="0" data-caption="LUMBAR Syndrome

What do you call a segmental lumbosacral hemangioma + spinal problems?? LUMBAR syndrome, a fairly new vascular anomaly syndrome. Important to be on the lookout to find other associated abnormalities &amp;amp; ensure correct management. 

Lower body hemangioma &amp;amp; other cutaneous defects 
Urogenital anomalies &amp;amp; Ulceration 
Myelopathy 
Bony deformities 
Anorectal malformation &amp;amp; Arterial anomalies 
Renal anomalies 

• Consider when you see segmental lumbosacral hemangioma + 1 other finding although exact criteria not specified to date 
• Thought to be lower body equivalent to PHACE syndrome 
• Arteriopathy is possible pathogenesis 
• MRI spine + MRI/MRA abd/pelvis typically recommended

Dr. Mark Mamlouk @ &amp;lt;a href=&amp;#34;https://twitter.com/MarkMamloukMD&amp;#34;&amp;gt;https://twitter.com/MarkMamloukMD&amp;lt;/a&amp;gt;

<a class="image-link image-link-6131 position-relative" data-bookmarked="false" data-bookmarks="0" data-caption="Dynamic CT Myelograms can help identify the source of spinal CSF Leaks. 
1. Place a sponge on CT &amp;amp; position prone Trendelenburg
2. Set up dynamic scan parameters to catch bolus
3. Inject 1 cc &amp;amp; scan right away
4. Look for dip in contrast
